newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Hollywood a sure winner in EU television showdown.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hollywood a sure winner in EU television showdown.

text.p: Luciana Castellina was feeling more than a little annoyed. She was unable to find a non-Hollywood film to see in Brussels, the self-styled capital of Europe, one recent Sunday afternoon.

The Italian Euro-MP leading a crusade against what she calls the "McDonaldisation" of culture says the incident shows why the European parliament will vote on Tuesday for stricter limits on U.S. films shown on European television.

"I wanted to see something else. I was not able. Either it was too far out or started at the wrong time. There was practically nothing other than "Independence Day," Castellina, chairwoman of the parliament's Culture Committee, told Reuters.
But the former journalist fears that Tinsel Town will emerge the winner when the parliament and EU capitals reach their "High Noon" showdown in the battle for Europe's screentime.

The parliament is expected to demand that the EU's controversial 1989 television without frontiers directive be revised to include mandatory limits on foreign -- read Hollywood -- films shown on European television.
It feels betrayed by EU governments, who, afraid of a damaging trade war with Washington, have already made clear they have no intention of putting the brakes on the prime U.S. export industry.

With an enormous monolingual home market, Hollywood can cover its production costs at home and then sell its films at a tenth of the price it would cost European film makers to make something similar.

So with eight out of 10 films shown on Europe's cinema screens and six out of 10 on television being American, the United States has clocked up a $4 billion trade surplus with Europe in the potentially job-spinning audiovisual sector.
Castellina and her Culture Committee say that, on democratic grounds, culture should not be left to the mercy of market forces and treated as a normal commodity like a potato or a washing machine.
"The people have the right to choose and not be oppressed by the big oligopoly that is Hollywood...It's not a question of Europe versus America, it's a question of Europe versus Hollywood," she said.

"This (Hollywood domination) will deprive the children of the world of their fantasies, their images and their heroes and they will become totally alientated. And I think that's there a risk that when someone becomes alienated they become socially irresponsible."

Even though the European market is large, it is multilingual and distribution of European films between one country and another is impeded by national broadcast quotas. French people tend to watch French rather than Finnish films.
"The problem is you won't have any exchange. There's some protection for the culture of your village and then there's McDonalds," said Castellina.

Over the past two years Castellina admits she has built up quite a friendship with the man she is trying to stop in his tracks, chairman of the Motion Picture Association Jack Valenti, with whom she crossed swords many times on the circuit of film festivals from Venice to Copenhagen to Beaune.
"We became friends with Mr Jack Valenti," she said. "It was hi Jack Valenti, ciao Jack Valenti. And we both repeated our arguments."
During the Uruguay Round of global world trade talks, the EU and Washington came to blows over a French-driven demand for a "cultural exception" to free trade rules to help protect European culture.

When the European parliament started to demand tougher quotas on Hollywood, Valenti set up a high-pressure lobbying base in Brussels and meetings of the previously low-profile Culture Committee became prime-time viewing for designer-suited lobbyists.
Europe's commercial television industry, fearing it would be forced into the expense of making home-made programmes rather than buying them cheap from America, joined the lobbying circus.
European film makers, directors and actors took the stage at the Culture Committee begging for EU action to prevent their industry literally bleeding to death.
But with the parliament likely to lose its fight for a clamp down on Hollywood, the chances are that Europe's film sector will have to turn its gaze on other European plans to help it.

EU capitals are dithering over a possible guarantee fund which the European Commission says could, on an initial injection of 200 million Ecus ($254 million), pump one billion Ecus ($1.61 billion) into the ailing European film sector.
